title: Arlington Central School District Board of Education v. Murphy
lead: After winning tuition reimbursement for their son, the Murphys seek the cost of an educational consultant, bringing competing readings of IDEA’s fee language to two appellate courts.

actors.name: Pearl and Theodore Murphy
actors.role: Parents who represented themselves and prevailed in their son’s educational-placement litigation.

actors.name: Joseph Murphy
actors.role: Child whose private-school tuition reimbursement was the underlying dispute.

actors.name: Arlington Central School District Board of Education
actors.role: School district opposing the consultant-fee award.

actors.name: Marilyn Arons
actors.role: Educational consultant with a master’s degree whose services produced the fee request.

proceedings: The parents prevailed on tuition reimbursement in March 2000; the Second Circuit affirmed the merits in 2002.
The district court later awarded $8,650 for qualifying consultation services.
The Second Circuit affirmed that fee award on March 29, 2005.
The Supreme Court reversed and remanded on June 26, 2006.
limits: The fee dispute is distinct from the already resolved placement merits. The account describes the original decisions and preserves differences among the six votes to reverse; it does not certify later statutory amendments.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent primary-source audit claimed.

sections.title: The Murphys win the educational-placement case and request consultant fees
sections.cue: What remained after the tuition dispute had ended?
paragraphs: Their son Joseph’s private-school tuition led Pearl and Theodore Murphy to seek reimbursement under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, or IDEA. Representing themselves, they won in district court in March 2000, and the Second Circuit affirmed that merits judgment in 2002. The later litigation did not reopen the appropriate educational placement.

In January and February 2003, the parents requested $29,350 for work by Marilyn Arons, an educational consultant with a master’s degree. IDEA, 20 U.S.C. § 1415(i)(3)(B), allowed discretionary awards of reasonable attorney’s fees as part of costs to prevailing parents. Their prevailing-party status was conceded. The disagreement concerned whether those words covered expert and consultant fees and, if so, which services qualified.

The district initially objected that Arons was a layperson unable to claim attorney’s fees, had not testified and lacked legal-procedure training, had inadequate time and market-rate evidence, and had worked in nonjudicial state proceedings outside the provision. Its initial expert objection accepted expert-fee availability but disputed her qualification. The categorical argument that IDEA did not authorize such fees became central on appeal.

sources.pinpoint: The dispute; Fee proceedings; Second Circuit opinion ¶¶ 3–9; 548 U.S. at 294

sections.title: Judge Haight distinguishes consultation from nonlawyer legal work
sections.cue: How did the requested amount become $8,650?
paragraphs: In a July 22, 2003 order, Judge Haight permitted compensation for expert consultation from the September 3, 1998 request for an impartial hearing through the March 1, 2000 merits decision. He excluded appellate work and legal services performed by a nonlawyer. Using $200 an hour as the market rate, the court ultimately awarded $8,650.

The court also rejected mileage because Arons had no driver’s license and denied interest because the parents had not paid the fees. The school district appealed on August 20, 2003. The Second Circuit reviewed statutory interpretation anew and reviewed the amount for abuse of discretion.

sections.title: Katzmann’s panel finds a reason to depart from the ordinary meaning of costs
sections.cue: Why did a conference report and a Casey footnote matter?
paragraphs: Judge Katzmann, writing for Judges Newman and Pooler, recognized that costs ordinarily do not include unrestricted professional fees of privately retained experts. Crawford Fitting required statutory witness-fee limits under 28 U.S.C. § 1821 absent explicit authorization or contract; West Virginia University Hospitals v. Casey construed the then-existing § 1988 attorney-fee wording to exclude expert fees. The panel therefore needed a reason to read IDEA differently.

It found that reason in IDEA’s conference report, which expressly described reasonable expert expenses, fees, and necessary tests or evaluations as included. Casey’s footnote 5 had discussed that report as an apparent attempt to depart from ordinary meaning and define a term of art. Katzmann’s panel read the footnote as recognizing a sufficiently expressed special meaning for IDEA, reinforced by the authority and specificity of a conference report.

Congress had responded to Casey by adding express expert-fee authority to § 1988 but had repeatedly amended IDEA, including in December 2004, without a comparable change. The panel inferred that Congress viewed IDEA’s existing formulation, illuminated by its conference report, as already covering experts. This was an inference from enactments and context, not an assertion that a failed proposal alone controlled meaning.

The panel also connected reimbursement to IDEA’s procedures and objectives. Assessing disabilities and proposed services often requires specialized help; parents may be accompanied and advised by knowledgeable or trained persons. Denying reimbursement could impede those protections in litigation seeking educational relief rather than damages. Compensation for consultation remained distinct from payment for unauthorized legal representation, consistent with the Third Circuit’s Arons decision.

The panel accepted the limited calculation below. It announced that future expert-fee applicants generally should keep contemporaneous time records but declined to impose that new expectation retroactively on Arons. Finding no abuse of discretion, it unanimously affirmed $8,650 on March 29, 2005. The assigned retrospective heading’s 2004 date does not describe the actual appellate decision.

sources.pinpoint: Second Circuit analysis and disposition; Assigned scope; 402 F.3d 332; opinion ¶¶ 11–26

sections.title: The Supreme Court asks what expense liability the enacted words impose
sections.cue: How do the Court’s textual and Spending Clause arguments fit together?
paragraphs: The Supreme Court took the fee dispute and reversed course. Justice Alito’s opinion treated IDEA as Spending Clause legislation: a state accepting federal money must knowingly and voluntarily accept the conditions. The relevant question was whether participating states received clear notice of liability for prevailing parents’ professional expert fees, not whether legislators expected that remedy or it might help the program.

The text gave no such notice. Costs was an established term for a restricted category of taxable items. Adding reasonable attorney’s fees did not also add expert fees. Nearby provisions addressed calculating and limiting attorney’s fees without a parallel expert-fee scheme, and required parental notices mentioned attorney’s fees but not expert liability. Sections 1920 and 1821 supplied the ordinary costs framework. The Court did not eliminate ordinary statutory witness allowances, including the attendance allowance; it rejected shifting professional expert fees through this IDEA provision.

The parents pointed to the 1986 Act’s direction that the General Accounting Office, or GAO, study attorney’s fees, costs, expenses, and hours worked by personnel including consultants. The Court responded that collecting information did not itself authorize reimbursement. A study could guide future legislation, and some expenses might be recoverable under state law. Avoiding surplusage was not an absolute command that converted the study into fee authority. The Court’s notes also distinguished statutory versions relevant to awards against parents.

Crawford Fitting and Casey reinforced the restricted reading. Casey’s footnote did not decide that the conference report correctly interpreted IDEA or furnished Spending Clause notice; it illustrated ordinary usage and an apparent effort to redefine it. General educational aims did not specify which expenses Congress chose to shift, particularly given fiscal concerns. Although the conference report plainly supported the parents, legislative history could not overcome the text, structure, and precedent. The GAO’s own statement about recoverable experts did not provide the necessary notice because it was not IDEA’s implementing agency.

sources.pinpoint: Supreme Court reasoning; 548 U.S. at 295–304 & nn.1–3

sections.title: Ginsburg supplies a sixth vote through ordinary interpretation
sections.cue: Which parts of the Court’s reasoning did she decline to join?
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg agreed with the result and joined the textual discussion at pages 296–298 and precedent analysis at pages 300–303. Congress had not enacted expert-fee language. The conference explanation might reflect sound policy but could not supply the missing statutory authorization. Her review of the conference and subsequent floor discussions found no further attention to expert fees comparable to the focus on overturning Smith v. Robinson’s attorney-fee restriction.

She rejected the categorical Spending Clause clear-notice premise for this remedy. IDEA also implemented Congress’s Fourteenth Amendment power. Pennhurst’s concern about an unexpected substantive condition differed from identifying remedies for breach of an accepted obligation, a distinction reflected in Bell v. New Jersey. She additionally noted the separate regulatory right to an independent educational evaluation at public expense; denying expert litigation fees under this clause did not abolish that entitlement.

sections.title: Breyer and Souter connect the fee clause to the enacted study and legislative history
sections.cue: Why did the dissenters find authorization in the statute as a whole?
paragraphs: Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Stevens and Souter, thought the result contradicted Congress’s clearly communicated objective. He traced the 1985–1986 bills, changing cost formulations, and bipartisan explanations of expert expenses. In his reading, the conference’s use of attorney’s fees as part of costs incorporated Marek v. Chesny without abandoning the repeatedly expressed inclusion of expert fees and necessary evaluations. Both Houses adopted the report without voiced disagreement on that point; his appendices reproduced the report and adoption proceedings.

Breyer linked this history to IDEA’s promise of a free appropriate education and parents’ role in enforcing it. Professional assessments and advice could be indispensable and expensive. Drawing on reimbursement precedents and family-resource information, he argued that denying fees could render protections practically unavailable even to parents who prevailed. That reasoning did not claim compensation for every service without qualification.

He also disputed the Spending Clause analysis. Pennhurst concerned an unforeseen substantive condition, whereas Bell and Jackson recognized remedies not exhaustively enumerated beforehand. Reasonable expert compensation differed from unexpected punitive damages and was modest beside IDEA’s possible educational obligations. Breyer accepted that the fee clause in isolation did not clearly grant expert fees, but rejected making that isolated observation decisive.

His structural anchor was the enacted GAO study of the new fee amendment’s effects. It referred to amounts of attorney’s fees, costs, and expenses awarded and included consultants’ hours. Read with the conference report, it supported a broader contextual meaning of costs. He questioned importing § 1920 as an exclusive definition when IDEA cases begin administratively and may proceed in state or federal court, potentially producing forum-dependent meanings.

Souter joined Breyer and separately stressed that the GAO provision had the same statutory dignity as the fee clause. It supplied a textual reason to consult the history, rather than an appeal to history detached from enacted law. Both would have upheld the expert-fee interpretation; Breyer urged continued use of text, structure, history, and purpose together.

sources.pinpoint: Breyer and Souter dissents; 548 U.S. at 308–30

sections.title: The fee award loses its statutory foundation
sections.cue: What did the six-to-three reversal leave untouched?
paragraphs: On June 26, 2006, the Supreme Court reversed the Second Circuit and remanded. Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas joined Alito’s opinion; Ginsburg’s separate position produced a six-to-three judgment but only five votes for the Spending Clause rationale. The ruling held that IDEA’s attorney-fee provision did not authorize professional expert-fee recovery. The parents’ earlier tuition-reimbursement victory was a different judgment.

Katzmann’s assigned retrospective account frames the disagreement around conference reports, later amendments, and statutory purpose. It also reports that the district first advanced its Spending Clause theory in the Supreme Court and that the parents objected to the timing. That is the retrospective account’s procedural characterization, not a separate Supreme Court holding about preservation. This story describes the original fee decisions and their disagreements without certifying later amendments or subsequent treatment.

sources.pinpoint: Supreme Court holding, judgment, and votes; Assigned context and limits; 548 U.S. at 293, 304–08
